title: A Message and an Ankle

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Tenth Saying: When the master cannot stand, the apprentice must.*

The haze at the edge of the Pale did not part so much as it dissolved, thinning into a grey mist that smelled of wet wool and distant rain. Isla was wiping a streak of mud from the brass sightglass when the sound reached them, a rhythmic, hoof-beat clip-clop that cut through the silence of the drift. A rider emerged from the fog, the horse lathered white with sweat, its breath steaming in the cool air. The rider was young, perhaps eighteen, dressed with a severity that seemed out of place in the scrubby, unmade landscape. She wore a plum-purple velvet coat with silver buttons that caught the faint light, cream breeches, and tall black boots so polished they reflected the grey sky. Her hair was a sleek black bob, cut sharp and precise, framing a face of pale, porcelain calm.

She reined the horse to a stop ten yards from the field desk, her hand steady on the bridle. She looked at the tents, the wagon, the chain stretched out across the Salt Flat, and finally at the four of them. Her gaze landed on Isla, lingered there for a fraction of a second, and then moved to Master Vasht, who stood with his hand on his walking stick, his face unreadable.

"Which of you," the rider asked, her voice clear and cool, "is in charge?"

Mags, who had been hanging her pot over the fire, looked up, a wad of porridge dough stuck to her cheek. "I am," she said, with absolute confidence. "I made the breakfast. Therefore, I hold the authority."

The rider’s eyebrow rose, a small, sharp movement. "I am Sera Quillon. I have been sent by the Lord Chancellor to assist with the survey of the Unmade." She dismounted with a fluid grace, tucking a stack of sealed sheets under one arm. She did not offer a hand, did not smile. She simply looked at the baseline, then at the instruments, and finally at Isla again, her expression one of mild, clinical interest. "The Chancellor sends his regards. He expects results by Midsummer. He also expects them to be... efficient."

Isla felt a cold prickle at the base of her neck. It was not fear, exactly. It was the sensation of a measurement error she had not yet identified. She stepped forward, her boots crunching on the salt crust. "And what is your role in this efficiency, Miss Quillon?"

Sera Quillon smiled, but it did not reach her eyes. "My role is to ensure the Guild’s reputation remains intact. I trust you have been making a good start."
pages.image: A young woman with a sleek black bob and plum-purple velvet coat stands beside a lathered horse in the grey mist, holding a stack of papers, looking down at Isla in her mustard coat and Master Vasht in his grey wool coat, who stands with a walking stick.

pages.text:
Sera Quillon did not wait to be invited to the field desk. She walked past Isla, her boots clicking on the wooden planks, and unrolled a fresh sheet of paper across the surface. She smoothed it down with a palm that seemed to erase the dust. Picking up Isla’s field-book, she flipped through the pages with a speed that blurred the numbers into streaks of ink.

"Baseline, one mile," she murmured, more to herself than to anyone else. "Measured twice. Chain and tape. Corrected for sag." She looked up, her dark eyes bright with a kind of detached amusement. "Impressive. Very thorough. And very slow."

Isla kept her voice level, though her hands were tight at her sides. "Thoroughness is not slowness, Miss Quillon. It is accuracy."

"Accuracy," Sera repeated, the word tasting strange in her mouth. "The Chancellor would say that accuracy is a luxury we can ill afford. He believes I could have covered this stretch in a week, using estimates and dead reckoning. The land does not move that fast."

"It does," Isla said, and the words came out harder than she intended. "I have seen it creep. I have seen a hill shift while I was reading a theodolite. If you estimate, you are not mapping the land. You are guessing at it. And the ink does not forgive guesses."

Sera raised an eyebrow, a gesture that seemed to be her default expression for disagreement. "The ink forgives what the hand intends. If your hand is steady, the line will be true. I have a steady hand, Miss Corrin. I have been told I am the fastest student in the Guild."

Master Vasht, who had been listening with his hands clasped behind his back, stepped forward. He did not look at Sera. His gaze fixed on the baseline, then drifted to the distant hilltop that served as their primary station.

"Miss Quillon," he said, his voice dry and courteous, like a sheet of paper being torn cleanly. "I would value a second opinion on the angles to that station. Could you take the readings? And perhaps show us your working? I am curious to see how the estimates compare to the measurements."

Sera’s smile tightened. "With pleasure. I will give you your results in ten minutes."

She turned to the sightglass, her movements quick and precise. Adjusting the screws with a flick of her wrist, she demonstrated a fluency that spoke of years of practice. Isla watched her hands, waiting for the tremor, the hesitation, the small human doubt that always preceded a true reading. It did not come.
pages.image: Sera Quillon in her purple coat sits at a wooden field desk, turning pages of a notebook rapidly, while Isla in her mustard coat stands with arms crossed and Master Vasht in his grey coat watches from the side, his expression neutral.

pages.text:
Sera Quillon read the angles with a speed that was almost frightening. She did not take the time to settle the bubble level, nor did she check the crosshairs twice, instead looking through the glass, turning the screw, and writing down the number before the tremor had a chance to reach her wrist. She did this again, and again, three times in rapid succession, her pencil scratching against the paper with a rhythmic urgency that seemed to defy the stillness of the field.

"There," she said, tapping the page with a slim silver rule. "Here are the angles. From the baseline, to the station. The triangle closes."

Isla took the book. The numbers were neat, small, and perfectly aligned in columns that looked as if they had been printed rather than written. They were also wrong.

"You did not read in both faces," Isla said, her voice quiet but steady.

Sera frowned. "Of course I did. Why would I not?"

"Because if you did, the second reading would be 180 degrees plus the first, and you have only recorded the direct angles, which means you have not checked the instrument for any residual error."

Sera’s face remained smooth, but her eyes narrowed into thin, sharp lines. "The instrument is calibrated. I checked it this morning."

"Calibrated is not the same as verified," Isla said, pointing to the numbers with an ink-stained finger. "Your angle to the station is off by four seconds of arc. It is a small error, the kind that would be nothing in a city of stone, but out here, with loose land and long distances, four seconds is enough to put the station a foot to the left, and a foot is enough to make the line bend."

Sera looked at the numbers, then at Isla. "It makes no practical difference. The land will not move a foot."

"It has moved three inches in the last hour," Mags said from the fire, where she was stirring the pot. "I watched it. It is like watching a pot of soup settle. It does not stop just because you are not looking."

Master Vasht cleared his throat. The sound was soft, but it filled the small space under the tent. "Miss Quillon," he said. "There is a saying among bridge-wrights that a bridge is only as strong as its weakest plank, and a survey is only as true as its least careful reading. The sentence 'it makes no practical difference' is the one that is found under every collapsed bridge."

Sera’s hand tightened on the edge of the desk, her knuckles whitening. "I am a surveyor. I do not make errors."

"No," Vasht agreed. "You make assumptions. And assumptions are not the same as measurements."
pages.image: Close up on a field-book page showing neat numbers, with Isla's ink-stained finger pointing to a specific column while Sera Quillon looks over her shoulder with a frown, her purple sleeve visible.

pages.text:
The accident happened an hour later, in the grey light that seemed to have no source. Joss was building a ramp for the wagon, a simple affair of timber and rope to cross a shallow ditch that had widened overnight, a small crevasse in the loose earth that was becoming more common as they moved deeper into the Unmade. He was testing the planks, walking across them with his boots, checking for strength, for flex, for the hidden rot that could fail under a load.

"The wood is good," he said, jumping down from the ramp. "It will hold the wagon."

Vasht, who had been standing nearby with his stick, nodded. "Good. Then we shall move the instruments."

Joss stepped onto the ramp again, placing his weight on the central plank. He was thinking of the tension, the compression, the way the forces traveled through the wood. He did not think of the knot, the small, dark circle in the grain that he had missed because it was on the underside, hidden by the shadow of the ditch.

The plank snapped.

It was not a dramatic break. It was a clean, sharp crack, like a bone breaking, and then the wood split, releasing a cloud of sawdust and air. Vasht, who had been stepping off the wagon onto the ramp, lost his footing. He fell, his hand gripping the edge of the wagon, but his momentum was too great. He swung, and then he dropped, landing hard on the loose earth below.

There was a sound, a short, sharp cry, and then silence.

Joss was there in a second, his face white. "Master Vasht! Master Vasht!"

Vasht lay on his side, his leg bent at an angle that was wrong, his face pale and tight with pain. He did not scream. He bit his lip, his eyes fixed on the sky.

Mags was next, dropping her pot, the fire hissing as water spilled from it. She knelt beside him, her hands moving with a speed that belied her size. "Breathe," she said, her voice steady. "Breathe, Master. Do not move."

Joss knelt on the other side, his hands hovering, not touching. "I missed the knot," he said, his voice hollow. "I missed the knot, and he fell."

Mags looked at him, her eyes hard. "You will not fix this with words, Joss. You will fix it with a splint. Get the tent pole. And the scarf."

Vasht closed his eyes, his breathing shallow. The fear in the air was thick, heavy, a physical thing that pressed against their chests. But Mags did not tremble. She did not cry. She moved with the precision of a surveyor, measuring the distance between the bone and the skin, calculating the angle, the support, the care.
pages.image: Mags in her teal jacket kneels beside Master Vasht, who lies on the ground with a bent leg, while Joss in his rust-red shirt kneels with his hands hovering in the air, looking terrified.

pages.text:
The wagon was turned around, its wheels creaking as they reversed it, the canvas flap pulled back to reveal the interior, which Mags converted into a field hospital with a speed that was almost magical. She hung a lantern from the hook, laid out a blanket, and placed a pillow under Vasht’s head. He was pale, his sweat shining on his forehead, but his eyes were open, and when he saw them, he smiled, a small, faint curve of the mouth.

"I am not dying," he said. "I am merely immobilized. There is a difference."

Mags splinted his leg with the tent pole and her blue scarf, tying it tight but not too tight, checking the circulation with a touch that was gentle and firm. "It is set," she said. "It will heal. But you will not be walking for a month."

Vasht looked at his leg, then at the field desk, then at Isla. The sun had set, and the stars were coming out, sharp and bright, scattered across the dark sky. The Unmade stretched out around them, a vast, blank sheet of silence.

"The commission," he said, his voice quiet but clear. "The Queen’s commission. It names 'Master Vasht or his designated hand.' I am the Master. But I am also the hand that is broken."

Sera Quillon stood by the wagon, her face unreadable. She had been quiet since the fall, her hands clasped in front of her, her eyes fixed on the ground. Now, she looked up, and for a moment, her expression was complicated, a mixture of surprise, and something else, something that looked like respect, or perhaps fear.

"Isla," Vasht said. "The survey is yours now. The Queen’s commission is a trust. It is not a possession. It is a promise. And a promise is a line that must be held."

Isla felt the sheer, crushing weight of it. She looked at the field-book, at the numbers, at the blank sheet of the Atlas hanging in the vault back in Vell. She looked at Sera, at Joss, at Mags. They were waiting. Not with pity, but with trust. A terrifying, fragile trust.

"I will need to see the plan again," Isla said. Her voice was steady, but her hands were shaking.

Vasht smiled, and this time, it reached his eyes. "You wrote it, Isla. You know where the lines go."

Isla took a breath, the air cold and sharp in her lungs. She picked up the field-book, the pages rustling in the night wind. She was ready. She was afraid. But she was ready.
pages.image: Isla in her mustard coat stands by the wagon, holding a field-book, looking at Master Vasht who sits inside with a splinted leg, while Sera Quillon stands in the shadows with a serious expression, the stars bright above.
